Argument for “They Are Old Friends Owing Each Other Favors”

Summary  
Far from a fixed criminal partnership, Peri and Gus Doran display the hallmarks of an informal fixer network: a series of barter‐like referrals in which each trades her or his unique channels and influence for a share of the proceeds. Their ease, casual credit, and rapid pivoting between multiple “projects” betray transactional friendship, not a committed conspiracy.

1. Initial Distrust and Reluctance  
• Peri’s surprise and refusal  
  – At first she is taken aback by Gus’ “Martian” pitch and insists “I saw him first!” <invalid_quote>“You must have heard wrong… I saw him first!”</invalid_quote> (Scene 1).  If she were his steady conspirator, she would not compete for the same “mark.”  
  – She only relents under pressure and for a one‐night gig: “Too bad I just got an awful headache…and can’t see Mr. Sastro tonight” <invalid_quote>“I just got… headache… Where you at, Gus?”</invalid_quote> (Scene 1).  This marker (“I owe you one”) is textbook social credit, not a pre‐arranged joint venture.

2. Fragmented “Assignments,” Not Unified Scheme  
• Multiple referral domains  
  – Peri supplies sexual companionship and social introductions. Gus separately offers underworld contacts, clothes, lodging, and business management. Each has independent pipelines: “You and Sam Wendt handle the routine…I will take the go‐between angle” <quote> You and Sam Wendt handle the routine. I will take the go-between  angle, </quote> (Scene 1) illustrating division of labor among freelancers.  
  – Gus says he “might get expensive” and “may be able” to find a con man, then shifts to tips about termination services: “if, say, you wanted somebody terminated… I could tell you a phone number.” <quote> I could tell you  a phone number."</quote> (Scene 2).  He hedges, showing he does “spot jobs,” not invests his own resources in a single massive scam.

3. Lack of Long‐Term Security Measures  
• Minimal vetting and casual security oaths  
  – Gus accepts Matheny’s information after a single “oath box” <invalid_quote>“I take a hundred security oaths a year… that formula… is the honest‐to‐zebra truth.”</invalid_quote> (Scene 2). A true conspirator requires strict screening and shared risk; Gus habitually trades with many clients under similar terms.  
  – No celebration of a completed joint con, no shared payout or common escape plan. Gus invites Doran’s girlfriend to celebrate, then departs to get girls—wide distribution of risk and reward.

4. Reciprocity, Not Exploitation Alone  
• Peri leverages her “private number” with “important men” <quote> some of the men who knew her private number were important.
</quote> (Scene 1); she expects Gus to “save” her favored client in return.  
• Gus trusts Peri’s referrals as he did before, shown by repeated use of her services and immediate offer to compensate her: Peri insists “Your share… is 500 000” <invalid_quote>“And your share… is 500 000 flat.”</invalid_quote> (Scene 1).  Commerce among friends, not exploitation of the unaware.  
• Both parties must repeatedly “earn” one another’s cooperation by providing new leads or switching to alternate “projects” when one client fails: a market‐like transaction model.

Refuting Debater_B’s “Fixed Conspirators” Claim  
A. Competitor Behavior  
  – Peri competes with Gus for the Martian’s attention and resents his overture: a partner would coordinate, not vie.  
B. Diverse, Disconnected Ventures  
  – They run separate lines (“Little Girl,” relics, Red Ankh, bucket shop, nightlife, murder referrals), often without mutual involvement.  
C. No Shared Exit Strategy or Revenue Pool  
  – Gus invests in Matheny with clothes, hotel, and drinks as a client acquisition cost, expecting commissions; Peri’s date yields only a one‐night fee. No joint “big con” profit split.  
D. Rapid Cold‐Shoulder When Unprofitable  
  – Peri’s readiness to abandon Matheny at the first sign of “headache,” and Gus’ willingness to move on to “other plans” whenever one line falters, signal freelancing, not loyalty.

Conclusion  
Their relationship is the prototypical “honest broker” network of a sophisticated urban environment: friends in the sense of repeat business acquaintances, freely exchanging favors to mutual advantage, with no binding conspiracy or shared criminal enterprise. The evidence of competition, minimal trust mechanisms, and myriad independent vignettes of service demonstrate a flexible, favor‐based alliance, not a single conjoined operation.

Argument for “They are conspiring con artists”

1. Every interaction is transactional, not reciprocal  
  a. Peri never offers personal aid without payment. She demands “your share of the million is one-third” (<quote>"Is five hundred thousand flat,"</quote>) only after Gus “gets this Martian” for her—a client she did not seek. If they were friends, she would repay Gus’s past favors before asking for her cut. Instead she immediately treats Matheny as hot property to split.  
  b. Gus similarly invests time, drinks, and costly hospitality (“room rate at the Jupiter-Astoria,” custom clothes from Schwartzherz, bar tabs) solely to sign Matheny as a client for his confidence operations. His subsequent pitch for a “confidence man” and introduction to murder services (<quote> I could tell you  a phone number."</quote>) only after securing oaths shows he views Matheny as a cash source, not a friend.  

2. Shared pattern of elaborate deceptions typical of professional cons  
  a. They maintain a cloak of “legitimate” fronts: The “Church of Choice” Bingo (<quote> This is a church!"</quote>) and “Little Girl” relic scheme (<quote>We erected the ruins fifty years ago</quote>) are classic long cons requiring cooperation. Such elaborate frauds demand specialized roles—Peri as the social lure, Gus as go-between—and would not be mounted by casual acquaintances.  
  b. Repeated reference to “security oaths” and using a “conditioner helmet” machine (<quote> I take a hundred security oaths a year, </quote>) indicates they operate in a criminal underworld. Friends trade personal loyalty; con artists require mechanical oaths to guard against betrayal.  

3. Lack of genuine personal rapport or mutual risk  
  a. Peri’s knee-jerk jealousy and impermanence: she flips between “I saw him first!” and “I just got a headache” whenever Gus offers a better take (<invalid_quote>“Badger?…break that date”</invalid_quote>). True partners do not abandon each other at the first sign of competition; con artists chase the richest mark.  
  b. Gus’s willingness to “forget” business when he spots a more lucrative avenue (from casual gambling to recruiting Peter as manager to seeking confidence man) shows opportunism, not loyalty to Peri or to any singular scheme. He never shares his own risks or costs with Peri; he simply “may get a cut.”  

4. Debater_A’s “favors” model fails to explain key facts  
  a. No record of Peri or Gus ever helping each other without profit. All favors are prefaced by “I need you…your share…five hundred thousand” or “this is on me” to entice future commission. Friendship would demand occasional unpaid reciprocity.  
  b. If they were established partners, they would coordinate one grand scheme. Instead they pitch multiple unconnected services (sexual liaisons, investment recruitment, murder-for-hire, security oaths), fragmenting their efforts to maximize disparate criminal opportunities. This is the hallmark of freelance operators pooling marks, not a single team.  
  c. Debater_A’s claim that Gus “owes” Peri rests on invalid inference: Peri’s reluctance over “Mr. Sastro” is clearly a ploy to preserve her high-price engagement for later, not evidence of ceding a “favor.” Then she cheerfully rejoins after Gus assures higher pay. That is client-shopping, not gratitude.

Conclusion  
The text depicts Gus and Peri as professional, opportunistic operators who assemble fronts to defraud Martians and Earthmen, then move on once the mark is spent. Their mutual dealings are strictly profit-driven, use covert security, and rely on covert criminal networks. No genuine altruism, shared risk, or friendship is ever shown. They are conspiratorial con artists, not friends owing favors.
